summary:
## TanStack Start: A Modern React Framework

TanStack Start is a full-stack framework built on **TanStack Router**, providing a compelling alternative to Next.js. It feels very similar in philosophy to **SvelteKit**, favoring RPC-style data fetching and a simpler mental model over the complexity of React Server Components (RSCs).

## Core Principles & Features

- **Isomorphic by Default**: All code can run on both the client and server unless specified otherwise, simplifying development.
- **Explicit Boundaries**: Use wrapper functions to define where code executes:
    - `createServerFunction`: For RPC calls that can be invoked from the client.
    - `createServerOnlyFunction`: For code that must *only* run on the server (e.g., accessing environment variables).
    - `createClientOnlyFunction`: For code that must *only* run on the client (e.g., accessing `localStorage`).
- **Loader Functions**: Similar to SvelteKit, `loader` functions fetch data before a component mounts. They run on the server for the initial page load (enabling SSR/SEO) and on the client for subsequent SPA-style navigations.
- **End-to-End Type Safety**: A crucial feature that provides a source of truth for data shapes across the client-server boundary.

## Data Fetching and Mutations

TanStack Start integrates seamlessly with **TanStack Query** (React Query), though it is not a required dependency.

- **Data Fetching Pattern**:
    1. Define a server function using `createServerFunction`.
    2. On the client, use the `useServerFunction` hook to get a data fetcher.
    3. Pass this fetcher to `useQuery`'s `queryFn` for a fully type-safe query.

> [!NOTE]
> By default, a mutation followed by a data refetch in the React example results in two network requests. The video contrasts this with a pattern in the Svelte ecosystem ("single-flight mutations") that achieves the same result in a single network hop for better efficiency.

## The Case Against Next.js RSCs

The video argues that the mental model for **React Server Components (RSCs)** in Next.js is overly complex, with confusing rules about component rendering locations, prop passing, and directives like `use client` and `use server`. TanStack Start offers a much simpler, more intuitive model reminiscent of the `tRPC` and pages router paradigm.

## Developer Experience

- **React Verbosity**: The example code uses `useCallback` to prevent function re-creation on re-renders, a common React pattern that adds boilerplate.

> [!TIP]
> The upcoming **React Compiler** is expected to automate memoization optimizations (`useCallback`, `useMemo`), which will significantly reduce boilerplate and simplify React code.

- **Excellent Tooling**: The framework benefits from the mature TanStack ecosystem, including powerful dev tools for **TanStack Router** and **TanStack Query** that aid in debugging.

## Project Viability

> [!IMPORTANT]
> TanStack Start is backed by serious companies and has a strong community, making it a viable and well-supported project for long-term use. It is not considered a risky or experimental choice.

## A Better React Framework?

I kind of accidentally became the Svelte guy, but I actually do really like React. There's some really good stuff there, and I think it's a very nice set of primitives for building web apps. The problem is there isn't really a good full-stack framework for React. There's Next.js, which is... I don't know, man. It's Next.js. What do you want me to say?

But TanStack Start is not Next.js, and it just hit release candidate, and it's really, really good. Initially, I was honestly just going to clone one of their example repos, play with it for a little bit, see how I felt about it, and then be done with it. But I actually ended up getting a little bit nerd sniped and spent a decent amount of time with this. I took the example to-do app that they ship with. I know to-do apps are boring and stupid. I agree. But at the end of the day, they do a really good job of showing all the different primitives these frameworks have, and I added some stuff to the one that they included, and I also ended up building the exact same thing in Svelte. So, I have the TanStack version, the Svelte version. I fully open-sourced both of these. They're linked down below.

And the thing that I really like about TanStack Start is it feels very similar to SvelteKit to me. They feel like very similar full-stack frameworks with very similar ways of doing things with the remote functions and the isomorphic rendering and all that stuff that just feels really, really good. Much better than the Next.js server component model that I'm just not that big a fan of.

## TanStack Start's Core Features

I know that TanStack Start will eventually support RSCs, and I'm sure that they'll find a really cool way of doing it. But as of right now, TanStack Start is basically just TanStack Router with a bunch of SSR stuff on top of it. And I'm not saying that to be like, "Oh, it's just TanStack Router. It's nothing special." No, TanStack Router is really, really good, and they did a really good job with these server-side primitives here. The full document SSR is great. Streaming is really good. These server routes are really nice. Server functions, I am a huge fan of. I love this pattern for data fetching and mutations. The middleware is great. Full-stack bundling, obviously. Universal deployment. And of course, end-to-end type safety. They have a really great type system, as you would expect all of the modern frameworks do, which is great.

I'm really glad that we have collectively settled on full-stack type safety being a non-negotiable at this point. It was really important in the past. It solved so many of the footguns that you would run into and made apps better. But now with AI writing a lot of code, having a source of truth on what is on your client, what is on your server, if you change one of those two, you get red lines. This is really, really important, and the TanStack ecosystem has historically had really good type safety. This framework is no exception.

## The Problem with Next.js Server Components

And if you're one of the people who feels very burned by Next.js app router, is not a fan of server components and all of the complexity that they add, I think that if you deeply understand that mental model, it can be fairly simple and understandable. There's a lot of weird stuff in there. Like the fact that you can have—you have your server components, which can return client components, but client components can also return server components, but not directly. You have to pass the server component as a prop down through the client component. And the client components only run on the client, except for when you first render the page, in which case they're going to be server-side rendered the first time. But then everything in the client component is going to be reactive and normal like a normal React component. But if you put special functions inside of your client components with a use server directive in there, that means that those can then be bundled to be actually server-side functions within your normal React components.

And you can see the mental illness in here and why people don't like this new mental model. If you understand it deeply, that's all really cool, and I've seen magical things with it. I understand why they went down this road. I feel like... I don't know. Maybe it's just because of the things that I started building with that I'm biased this way. Like my first real foray into like building real apps was the OG create T3 app world, where it was Next.js pages router plus tRPC. So, I'm very used to that like RPC functions to get and mutate my data.

Within each route, you go through and you create a new file route. This is the index route of my app. I mount a component in here, which is going to be like the page component or whatever. Then we have our loader function, which is very similar to the load functions in Svelte. These are basically just functions that get called before the component mounts, so that we have that data at runtime. This can run on both the client and the server, which I'll talk about in a second. I actually really like the way they handled and did all that stuff. And then down here, we have our actual component, where we can grab our loader data, we can use a bunch of server functions, we can use a bunch of TanStack Query primitives here, because it's a really great way of dealing with data, and then it's a normal React component. There's no weird use client, no weird use server. This will feel like a normal React SPA if you want it to, with a bunch of type safety data fetching primitives built into it. I'm a big fan of the way they did this.

## Isomorphic by Default: The Execution Model

This page in their docs is actually the entire reason I wanted to make this video, where they talked about their execution model. And the core principle here is isomorphic by default. Basically, what this means is that all of your code can be run on both the client and the server, unless you specify otherwise. So, this is honestly very similar to what's happening in modern Next.js, where by default, a server component will just run on the server. But then when you put the use client tag on there, that means that this is code that can run on the client. And if you put server only on there, you do the import server only, that is saying that this is code that can only be executed on the server.

When you're working with these modern full-stack JavaScript frameworks, you have to explicitly define the boundaries between client and server. Like, what code runs on the client, what code runs on the server, cuz we are importing these things back and forth and doing a bunch of magic under the hood to make all that work. There's a whole drama, I think it was like last week or the week before, where Vercel introduced the use workflow decorator thing. And then that like magic string of use workflow will tell the compiler that this is workflow code, and then at compile time, that code will get put into the right workflow box.

They're doing something similar here. Just instead of using use client or use server, we're doing create server function. So, we want an RPC call, you put the code in a create server function. If you want a server only function for something like getting an environment variable, you do create server only function. There's very similar stuff for client stuff. So, like we need to have a utility function for local storage, we wrap that in a create client only function, so that if we try and put that on the server, it'll crash.

And then everything else is isomorphic. So, like this format price can run on both the client and the server. This loader will run both during SSR. So, if you needed to do some SEO stuff on your page, like fetching the details of a product or whatever, you can put that in the loader, that'll be SSR'd and instantly hydrated as soon as it's there for good SEO crawling. And then also, you get the good SPA navigation experience, where instead of having to do a network hop off to the server to fetch the data and then block on the client before we can see the next page, it will do the SPA thing, where we will instantly navigate and then run this loader on the client. And in the actual code base here, I'm doing await get server to-dos, which means that if it's running on the server, it can just like call that function, it's fine. If it's doing it on the client, you can use the built-in primitives for calling these server functions to do that all client-side. It's a really nice mental model. SvelteKit does a very similar thing. I have no idea how Next does things, but that's the way these two do it, and that's the way I like things to actually work.

## Type-Safe Data Fetching with React Query

And then the actual code of this to-do app is like pretty much exactly what you would expect. If you're used to tRPC or normal client-side React code, probably using React Query. If you're not using React Query with React, I don't really know what you're doing. All of this just kind of works together nicely. We define our server functions. So, I have this get server to-dos. This is just a simulated example with hard-coded to-dos on the server that are saved in memory. Nothing special.

We're grabbing our to-dos off of the server, returning them right here. And then on the client, we call this use server function hook, which will get us basically a data fetcher here, kind of, that we can then pass into this use query as our query function to get fully type-safe data on our to-dos. Kind of like tRPC, but with slightly extra steps, if that makes any sense. I understand why they did it this way instead of just doing like a direct use server function returning a use query. This really feels like basically what they're doing is they're taking all of the really good primitives that already exist in the TanStack ecosystem, effectively, with TanStack Query, TanStack Router, all the way to get type-safe use query without forcing you to use React Query. React Query is not a built-in dep to TanStack Start, but it's something that you can use in a very first-class way, if that makes any sense. I actually really respect and like this approach a lot.

## Handling Mutations & SvelteKit Comparison

Mutations are very similar. You can just call add to-do, as in it just feels like a function here, because if you look at the actual code here, we're doing the input validator to say, "Hey, this needs to have a name of string." On the server, this zod validator will be called on here. So, we pass in bad data, it will error. Then we have our handler here to grab all our stuff. We return our to-do, and we get full type safety on all this. Whole thing just works like a React app. It's great.

And if we go over to the SvelteKit app here, you'll notice that they look and feel very, very similar. At the top here, I have this to-dos query, which is wrapped in a derived. The reason I'm wrapping it in a derived is so that whenever we change the data from remote get to-dos, which we can do, we can have that automatically refetch for us, which is really convenient. This to-dos query will update, so then these to-dos will become reactive, which means that anywhere where we call these within like a derived or within the markup, a signal will basically get bound there, and then this data will update. So, anytime we update this data, this will get updated, this will get updated. And the server-side code for this also looks very similar. Uh the difference is instead of just being like one raw primitive for making server functions, that's basically just a type-safe wrapper around REST, they have the query, the command, the um form for like a form action type thing, which allows you to do some other really, really cool things.

## Single-Flight Mutations: A Svelte Advantage

I'm not going to make this a Svelte propaganda video. There is actually Okay, there's one thing that I do want to talk about on the Svelte side that I think is a lot better, uh which is the single flight mutations. Because if you look at this, when I go to the network tab, and I'm just going to do put some random stuff in here, hit add, you're going to see that data instantly got updated, but there was only one network hop here. Where if you look at the payload response here, we're getting our result of the submission, but we're also getting this refreshes. So, it's passing in the refresh data for to-dos. And since we're wrapping this in a derived, we're getting new data into this to-dos query, and everything just instantly gets updated in one network hop. And the only code you have to write to do this is this. It's literally just remote get to-dos.refresh.

And in one network hop, we will get fully synced up state. It's a really, really convenient way of handling and doing all this stuff. You can hack around and do something similar to this in the TanStack example. You can see in the network tab, if I go over here, do the same thing, hit enter, there's two network requests. The first one is going to be the post to like save it here, so you can see the new one I just made. And then this is fetching all the to-dos again. So, we're doing two network requests every time, and you could hack this so that in the on success of the mutation, you would do get the data back. So, you can see you're getting your to-do back here with full type safety. We could mutate this, or we could have a second to-do state variable that we then update to only do like one network round trip or whatever, or do some optimistic updates. There's a lot of ways you can get around this. And honestly, I'm sure that there will be React experts who are like, "No, use query has a thing where you can just directly update the data in there. You don't have to do this." And if that's the case, awesome. But, I personally just find that can ultimately result in some weird split-brain things where I don't really want to have a client-side state and a server-side state for something like this. I'd much rather have it just be whenever I finish this mutation and create a new one, I call refetch, I get the data back in here, and then this is the source of truth for my to-dos. I don't want a second one that I'm constantly updating back and forth. I just want one singular place in my brain where I'm dealing with this. It wouldn't be too hard to hack around in a basic example like this, but in a real-world app, having your one source of truth constantly get updated correctly like this in one network request is really, really cool. They did a great job with this.

## React Verbosity and the Promise of React Compiler

But honestly, outside of that one complaint, this is definitely, in my opinion at least, the best way to write React code for the web right now. These primitives feel really, really good. The code is just going to be a bit more verbose in here than something like a Svelte or even like a Nuxt, just because of the nature of what React is. React compiler does help with a lot of this. Like, to be fair, like this example looks worse than it probably should because I'm wrapping all of these mutations in a use callback here because if you're not familiar with the React mental model, effectively, every single time we change a state variable within this TanStack query demo, we're going to rerun this function with the new state. So, it's like, it is truly the UI as a function of state thing, where the way React re-renders stuff is it will recall this entire function, which means it will recreate all of these functions unless we wrap them in a use callback and give a dependency array here, where unless we're changing mutate reset to-dos, we are not going to recreate this function.

It's... React compiler fixes this, where you don't have to write this anymore. The compiler will automatically do these optimizations for you. It will put the use callbacks, it'll do the use memos, handle all those things for you, which is great. I just wanted to like show what this does actually look like if you're doing this in the way that's technically correct.

## Developer Experience and Ecosystem Support

There's also some really cool stuff in here with their like dev tools system, because TanStack is such a good ecosystem of packages that's very well maintained. They have these dev tools for TanStack router and for TanStack query. Where we look at TanStack query here, we can see our to-dos in here. We can see the data in here. We can call a refetch. We can call a reset. We can trigger a loading state. There's a lot of different things we can do in here to actually debug and test this. They also have a really good set of examples in the docs on how to do stuff with React query, with Clerk auth, DIY auth, Convex, WorkOS, Material UI, static rendering, Cloudflare. Like, this is a very well-supported and well-put-together project that I think has a very bright future. I know a concern that a lot of people would probably have with something like this is, "Oh, is it going to be supported in the long term? Is this something that I should be betting on?" There are enough companies in here that are very real and very serious putting a lot of money behind this that I do not think that this is going anywhere.

## Final Verdict and the Future with RSCs

This is a very, very good project that I'm very happy to see. I want to see patterns like this adopted more across the web. It just makes building things easier and more pleasant. I am extremely curious to see what their RSCs implementation ends up looking like, cuz they haven't done that yet, but they did say that they're exploring it right now. There's some weird limitations with like bundlers and stuff like that. I was I was listening to an interview with Tanner earlier, where apparently there's like I didn't even know this. RSCs are very bizarre in the fact that they only really work in Turbo Pack and Next.js right now. They've done some hacks to get them working in React router, what that was demoed at React Conf, is really cool. There are some cool stuff you can do with those, but it's not quite ready for Vite yet. They're still figuring out how to do that, what they want it to look like. It's going to come eventually. Curious to see what it looks like.

Even RSCs aside, this is the React framework that I would pick for the web. And if you are sick of Next.js, you should definitely go try this.
